analysis: Examined three changed files. (1) ProviderCore.swift: version bump 0.10.12 to 0.10.13 only; no security behavior change. (2) GenerationLoopGuardPolicy.swift (head lines 61-88): resolve() gains an optional exitThinking parameter (default nil) passed to GenerationLoopGuard. Gating is unchanged: the guard is skipped for token constraints, forced tool calls, JSON response formats and parsers that accept bare JSON. It operates on the provider's local output stream after decryption, adds no network, key, attestation or storage surface, and does not change the TB-002 encryption path (T-008). The new exit-thinking behavior is implemented in GenerationLoopGuard and GenerationLoopExitThinking, which were not supplied, so I could not check whether it injects or alters tokens, or whether it touches the prefix cache (T-041). It affects output quality and availability, not confidentiality as far as visible. (3) LaunchAgent.swift (head lines 421-423, 454-455): two env keys, DARKBLOOM_LOOP_GUARD and the GenerationLoopExitThinkingPolicy key, are added to the launchd passthrough allowlist inferencePassthroughEnvKeys, which flows into passthroughEnvKeys and passthroughEnvironment. Values are copied from the installing shell into the user-owned LaunchAgent plist. Those are inference-behavior toggles only. The operator already controls the environment (ADV-001 and TB-003 assume operator-level control), and the keys only change the repetition-guard model list or turn it off. Neither key leaks secrets, and neither is a worker, attestation or App Attest opt-in key (the allowlist for those stays separate and unchanged). A malicious operator disabling the guard only degrades their own served output quality, which is the same class as T-007. I found no regression against the threat model. Residual question: whether the unseen GenerationLoopGuard exit-thinking code logs or retains prompt or output text, or alters the emitted stream in a way that affects T-056 style overclaims; this should be checked in the unsupplied source.
